messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Cold Temperature: Cold, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Linh

Linh was forty-two when the infection came. She had been a project manager at a mid-sized logistics firm for eleven years, the kind of woman her colleagues relied on to keep timelines tight and stakeholders aligned. She worked from a glass-walled office on the third floor, her calendar visible to anyone passing by, her door always open except when she was on calls. Her husband, Michael, was a high school teacher. They had been married eighteen years. They had no children, though they had tried for many years before accepting that it would not happen. Her work had become, in a quiet way, the place where she felt most essential.

In January, she developed what seemed like a routine urinary tract infection. Within forty-eight hours, the infection had spread into her bloodstream. She remembered the moment in her home office when the fever spiked so violently that she could not hold her mouse. The cold came next—not the pleasant cool of an air-conditioned room, but a bone-deep cold that made her teeth chatter so hard she feared they would crack. Michael drove her to the emergency department at 2 a.m. She remembered the smell of the hospital: something chemical and institutional, layered beneath the fainter scent of human illness. She remembered the IV line being inserted, the needle sliding into her arm, the sensation of cold saline entering her vein. She remembered, very clearly, the moment a resident told her she was in septic shock and that if she had waited another few hours, she would likely have died.

What came after was less clear. She had spent nine days in the ICU, though entire stretches of it had simply vanished from her memory. She knew, because the hospital records said so, that her blood pressure had crashed twice. She knew she had been on three different antibiotics. She knew, because Michael had told her afterward with his eyes red, that she had not recognized him for two of those days. But the experience itself felt unreal, like something that had happened to someone else, or like a story she had read rather than lived through. The clarity she did have was fragmentary and strange: she could see the face of a particular nurse, could remember the exact shade of blue of the ICU gown, could recall with perfect precision the sensation of the catheter, but entire conversations and procedures existed for her now only as a kind of emotional residue—a terror without a face, a helplessness without a specific moment to attach it to.

She had been home for six weeks when the smell came. Michael was cooking, and he had opened a window because the kitchen was warm. The cold air that rushed in carried the faint scent of the hospital's cleaning solution—or something like it—and Linh had felt her heart rate spike so violently that she had to sit down. She had not been able to explain it to Michael in the moment. The smell had triggered not a memory but a pure sensation of dread, a conviction that something terrible was about to happen, even though she was safe in her own kitchen.

She had begun, after that, to monitor her thoughts with an intensity that exhausted her. Every time she felt a flutter of anxiety, she would pause and ask herself: Is this real worry or am I starting to go crazy? The question had become a constant companion. She was terrified that the sepsis had damaged her mind, that the high fevers had left her fundamentally altered. She had not told anyone this fear—not even Michael—because speaking it aloud seemed like it might make it true.

By April, she had stopped going to her annual physical. She had cancelled a dentist appointment. When Michael had suggested she see her primary care physician about the persistent fatigue she felt, she had refused. The thought of sitting in a medical office, of seeing medical equipment, of being examined—it had become intolerable. She had come to believe that her body had been permanently compromised, that any further medical intervention would only confirm how damaged she was.

At work, her performance had begun to slip. She had missed two team meetings because she could not face the drive across town on a cold morning—the cold seemed to carry with it a premonition of illness, of losing control. Her director had noticed. In May, he had called her into his office and asked if everything was all right. She had said yes, but she had known, even as she said it, that she was failing at the one thing she had always been able to do well. Her life, she had come to believe, had been destroyed. The person she had been before January—competent, reliable, present—seemed to have died in that ICU, and what remained was someone fragile and unreliable, someone whose body could betray her at any moment.

It was Michael who finally insisted she call a therapist. He had found her one evening sitting in the dark in their bedroom, unable to explain why she could not come downstairs for dinner. She had agreed, not because she believed therapy could help, but because she had begun to recognize that the monitoring of her own mind was becoming a kind of torture, and she was desperate for it to stop.
